title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 13
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: The Printing Press and Knowledge Revolution
passages.text:
The invention of the movable type printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in the mid-fifteenth century fundamentally transformed the transmission and democratization of knowledge across Europe. Before the printing press, books were painstakingly copied by hand, typically by monastic scribes working in scriptoriums. This labour-intensive process meant that books were extraordinarily expensive and consequently rare; a single manuscript could take months to complete and command prices equivalent to several months' wages for an ordinary craftsman. The circulation of knowledge was therefore severely restricted to wealthy nobility, the clergy, and a small scholarly elite.

Gutenberg's innovation, which combined movable metal type with a mechanical press and oil-based ink, made mass production of printed materials economically feasible. Within fifty years of Gutenberg's first printed Bible in 1455, printing presses had been established in over two hundred cities across Europe, and estimates suggest that more books were produced in this half-century than had been manufactured by hand during the entire previous millennium. This explosive proliferation of printed materials fundamentally altered both the quantity and character of information circulating through European society.

The availability of identical, standardised copies transformed scholarly practices. Before printing, scholars had to travel to remote libraries to consult unique manuscripts, each potentially containing errors introduced by copyists. Printed books created the possibility of a shared scholarly corpus: multiple scholars could now study the exact same text, compare editions, and identify corruptions introduced through centuries of hand-copying. This standardisation contributed significantly to the development of scientific methodology, as researchers could replicate and verify observations against the same authoritative sources.

The printing press also catalysed the emergence of the reading public. As book prices gradually declined and literacy rates increased, reading shifted from an elite activity performed aloud in groups to a more solitary, private practice. The rise of silent reading and individual book ownership began to reshape cultural and intellectual life. Coffee houses and lending libraries became spaces where middle-class readers gathered to discuss printed materials, fostering the emergence of public opinion and informed debate on matters of governance and religion.

The religious upheaval of the Protestant Reformation was profoundly enabled by the printing press. Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses, printed and distributed widely in 1517, would almost certainly have remained confined to academic circles had they existed only in manuscript form. The ability to produce thousands of identical copies of theological arguments allowed the Reformation to spread with unprecedented speed across linguistic and political boundaries, challenging the monopoly on biblical interpretation that the Roman Catholic Church had long enjoyed.

The transition from manuscript to print culture also introduced new challenges. Printed books could spread misinformation and heretical ideas as efficiently as accurate scholarship. Governments and religious authorities, alarmed by the loss of control over information, began implementing censorship regimes and creating indices of prohibited books. The tension between the liberating potential of printing and the desire to restrict dangerous knowledge persists to this day, though now manifested in debates over digital content and information access on the internet.

passages.title: Photosynthesis and the Carbon Cycle
passages.text:
Photosynthesis represents one of the most important biochemical processes on Earth. Through this mechanism, autotrophic organisms — principally plants, algae, and certain bacteria — capture energy from sunlight and convert it into chemical energy stored in glucose and other organic compounds. This conversion of radiant energy into chemical energy is the foundation of nearly all life on Earth, as heterotrophic organisms ultimately depend on photosynthetically produced food for their survival.

The process occurs in two main stages: the light-dependent reactions and the light-independent reactions, commonly known as the Calvin cycle. During the light-dependent reactions, which take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, photons are absorbed by chlorophyll and other pigments. This energy excites electrons, driving them through a chain of protein complexes. The energy released by this electron transport is used to pump protons across the thylakoid membrane, creating a concentration gradient that powers the synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH). Both of these molecules serve as energy carriers in the light-independent reactions.

The Calvin cycle, occurring in the stroma of the chloroplast, utilizes the ATP and NADPH produced during the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase, commonly abbreviated as RuBisCO, catalyzes the initial carboxylation of a five-carbon sugar, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. This produces an unstable six-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two three-carbon molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate. Through a series of reduction and rearrangement steps, these molecules are gradually converted into glucose while regenerating the original five-carbon acceptor molecule.

Photosynthesis plays a central role in the global carbon cycle, the biogeochemical process that moves carbon between the atmosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere. During photosynthesis, plants and other autotrophs extract carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, incorporating the carbon into organic tissues. This process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores it in biomass. Conversely, cellular respiration in plants, animals, and decomposers returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, completing the cycle.

The balance between photosynthetic carbon fixation and respiratory carbon release has been relatively stable for much of Earth's geological history, resulting in relatively constant atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations. However, the combustion of fossil fuels — coal, oil, and natural gas — which are ancient deposits of organic carbon formed from photosynthetically produced biomass — has dramatically accelerated the release of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere over the past two centuries. This disturbance of the carbon cycle is driving the accumulation of atmospheric carbon dioxide and its consequent effects on global climate.

Climate-related changes have already begun affecting photosynthetic rates and patterns globally. Altered precipitation patterns and rising temperatures are changing the geographic distribution of photosynthetically productive ecosystems. Some regions are experiencing extended growing seasons, potentially increasing annual photosynthetic productivity, while other regions are becoming drier and less hospitable to plant growth. These shifts threaten agricultural productivity in some areas and demonstrate the profound interconnection between Earth's biogeochemical cycles and the stability of human civilization.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why were books extraordinarily expensive before the printing press?
questions.correctAnswer: They were painstakingly copied by hand, which was labour-intensive
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states 'books were painstakingly copied by hand' and that 'a single manuscript could take months to complete.'
options: Paper had not been invented
They were painstakingly copied by hand, which was labour-intensive
Most people could not read
Religious authorities banned distribution

questions.prompt: The word 'democratization' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Democratization of knowledge' refers to making knowledge available to common people rather than just elites.
options: establishing political systems
making accessible to ordinary people
rapid multiplication of ideas
written documentation

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, approximately how many cities had printing presses within fifty years of Gutenberg's first Bible?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states 'printing presses had been established in over two hundred cities across Europe.'
options: Fewer than fifty cities
Approximately one hundred cities
Over two hundred cities
Over five hundred cities

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the impact of standardised printing on scholarly work?
questions.correctAnswer: It enabled scholars to build on shared, reliable sources and develop scientific methodology
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that standardised copies allowed scholars to 'compare editions, identify corruptions' and that this 'contributed significantly to the development of scientific methodology.'
options: It reduced the importance of library research
It enabled scholars to build on shared, reliable sources and develop scientific methodology
It made scholarly work less rigorous
It eliminated the need for original investigation

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention coffee houses and lending libraries in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate how printing enabled a new reading public and informed public debate
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes these spaces as where 'public opinion and informed debate' emerged among middle-class readers.
options: To argue that coffee houses were more important than printing
To illustrate how printing enabled a new reading public and informed public debate
To show that most people lived in urban areas
To suggest that reading remained an elite activity

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, which of the following is NOT stated as a consequence of the printing press regarding the Reformation?
questions.correctAnswer: It prevented theological arguments from spreading beyond Europe
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states the Reformation spread 'across linguistic and political boundaries,' not that it was prevented.
options: It allowed Luther's Ninety-Five Theses to spread widely
It enabled the Reformation to spread across linguistic boundaries
It prevented theological arguments from spreading beyond Europe
It challenged the Catholic Church's monopoly on interpretation

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, when were Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses printed and distributed?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 explicitly states 'Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses, printed and distributed widely in 1517.'

questions.prompt: The word 'misinformation' in paragraph 6 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Misinformation' refers to false or misleading information, contrasted with 'accurate scholarship.'
options: detailed documentation
false or inaccurate information
strictly religious content
unauthorized publications

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in: 'The ability to produce thousands of identical copies of theological arguments allowed the Reformation to spread with unprecedented speed across linguistic and political boundaries.'
questions.correctAnswer: Mass printing of religious texts enabled the Reformation to spread rapidly across many regions and languages
questions.explanation: The sentence conveys that widespread printing capability allowed the Reformation's rapid spread across different language groups and political boundaries.
options: The Reformation began simultaneously in many different countries
Mass printing of religious texts enabled the Reformation to spread rapidly across many regions and languages
Theological arguments were understood only in certain languages
The Catholic Church eagerly promoted the use of printing technology

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: The passage's main themes are: printing revolutionised book production (A), standardisation benefited scholarship (C), and printing enabled religious and social upheaval but also spread misinformation (E).
options: A. The printing press dramatically increased book production and accessibility, shifting knowledge from elites to broader populations.
B. Monastic scribes successfully adapted to printing technology and maintained their social status.
C. Standardised printed texts enabled scholars to work collaboratively and contributed to scientific methodology.
D. Martin Luther invented the printing press to support his theological arguments.
E. The printing press enabled rapid spread of ideas like the Reformation but also allowed misinformation, prompting censorship.
F. Reading remained exclusively a group activity performed aloud after the printing press was invented.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the fundamental role of photosynthesis in life on Earth?
questions.correctAnswer: It converts solar energy into chemical energy that supports nearly all life
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that photosynthesis is 'the foundation of nearly all life on Earth' because it converts light energy into chemical energy.
options: It produces oxygen exclusively for animals
It converts solar energy into chemical energy that supports nearly all life
It absorbs all atmospheric carbon dioxide
It regulates Earth's temperature

questions.prompt: The word 'catalyzes' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: speeds up or enables a reaction
questions.explanation: 'Catalyzes' means to act as a catalyst, which accelerates or facilitates a chemical process.
options: initiates plant growth
speeds up or enables a reaction
absorbs light energy
creates new molecules

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what role do ATP and NADPH play in the Calvin cycle?
questions.correctAnswer: They serve as energy carriers that power carbon dioxide fixation
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that ATP and NADPH 'serve as energy carriers in the light-independent reactions' (Calvin cycle).
options: They capture photons from sunlight
They serve as energy carriers that power carbon dioxide fixation
They regenerate chlorophyll
They prevent electron transport

questions.prompt: Why does the author explain RuBisCO's role in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate the first step of carbon dioxide fixation in the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes RuBisCO as catalysing 'the initial carboxylation,' which is the first step of CO2 fixation.
options: To show that the Calvin cycle is the most complex process
To illustrate the first step of carbon dioxide fixation in the Calvin cycle
To explain why photosynthesis requires sunlight
To show that enzymes are unnecessary

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about the relationship between photosynthesis and the carbon cycle?
questions.correctAnswer: Photosynthesis removes carbon from atmosphere while respiration returns it, maintaining natural balance
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that 'plants extract carbon dioxide from the atmosphere' while 'respiration returns carbon dioxide, completing the cycle.'
options: Photosynthesis and respiration are unrelated
The carbon cycle occurs only in plants
Photosynthesis removes carbon from atmosphere while respiration returns it, maintaining natural balance
Carbon dioxide levels never change in the atmosphere

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, what is causing an imbalance in the natural carbon cycle?
questions.correctAnswer: The combustion of fossil fuels has accelerated carbon dioxide release
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states 'the combustion of fossil fuels has dramatically accelerated the release of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.'
options: Increased plant growth due to higher temperatures
A reduction in photosynthetic organisms
The combustion of fossil fuels has accelerated carbon dioxide release
Changes to Earth's atmospheric composition long ago

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 6, which of the following is NOT mentioned as an effect of climate change on photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: A decrease in photosynthetic productivity in all regions globally
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6 states some regions have 'extended growing seasons' while others become drier—not uniform global decrease.
options: Changes in precipitation patterns
Rising temperatures affecting plant distribution
Extended growing seasons in some regions
A decrease in photosynthetic productivity in all regions globally

questions.prompt: The word 'disturbance' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Disturbance of the carbon cycle' refers to a disruption of the natural equilibrium.
options: a severe weather event
disruption of normal balance
an increase in productivity
the formation of fossil fuels

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in: 'Climate-related changes have already begun affecting photosynthetic rates and patterns globally, with some regions experiencing extended growing seasons while others become less hospitable to plant growth.'
questions.correctAnswer: Climate change is affecting plant growth differently in different regions
questions.explanation: The sentence conveys uneven impacts across regions—some improving, others declining.
options: All regions globally are experiencing longer growing seasons
Climate change is affecting plant growth differently in different regions
Growing seasons have been eliminated everywhere
Climate has no effect on plant growth patterns

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.explanation: The main themes are: photosynthesis's fundamental role (A), the carbon cycle's importance (D), and climate disruption of these processes (F).
options: A. Photosynthesis converts solar energy into chemical energy and is the foundation of nearly all life on Earth.
B. The Calvin cycle is the only phase of photosynthesis and occurs exclusively in thylakoid membranes.
C. RuBisCO is the only enzyme in photosynthesis.
D. Photosynthesis plays a central role in the global carbon cycle by removing atmospheric CO2 and storing it in biomass.
E. Fossil fuels are the only source of atmospheric carbon dioxide.

F. Climate change is already altering photosynthetic rates and patterns, with uneven impacts threatening agriculture and demonstrating the interconnection between biogeochemical cycles and human wellbeing.
